summary: Defines a method for a device to tell a DHCPv6 server that it has one or more self-generated or statically configured addresses. This lets the server know about addresses it did not hand out.

plainLanguage.summary: Some devices pick their own address instead of being given one. This lets them quietly tell the network's address office, so it has a full list.

questions: how to register self-generated ipv6 addresses
how do i register slaac addresses with dhcpv6
subtitle: How a device tells a DHCPv6 server about the IPv6 addresses it made up for itself, so logs stay complete.

tldr.problem: Networks often use DHCP logs to find out which device had which address. For IPv6, devices usually build their own addresses with SLAAC, so the DHCPv6 server never learns about them.
tldr.mechanism: A client first checks that the server supports the feature using a new option, then multicasts an ADDR-REG-INFORM message for each self-generated or static address. The server logs it and answers with ADDR-REG-REPLY.
tldr.outcome: DHCPv6 infrastructure can know about self-assigned addresses, giving IPv6 the same troubleshooting and forensics trail that IPv4 DHCP logs provide. It is informational and must not be used for authentication or authorization.

today: RFC 9686 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024. It has not been obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

sections.title: Why Servers Need to Know
sections.content:
In enterprise networks it is common to use IPv4 DHCP logs for troubleshooting and forensics. A help desk can look up a printer's IPv4 address from its MAC address, and a security team can find which laptop held an address when suspicious traffic appeared in firewall logs.

That works for IPv4 because most addresses are either assigned by DHCP or statically configured by the operator. For IPv6, devices often configure their own addresses through Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), so the DHCPv6 server has no record of them. This document gives a device a way to inform the DHCPv6 server of such an address, providing parity with IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: If the school office only writes down the lockers it assigned, it cannot tell who is using a locker a student picked alone. This lets students report their own locker.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
DHCPv6 itself is the registration protocol, and a DHCPv6 server acts as the address registration server. The RFC adds a new option, OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE, which shows that a server supports the mechanism.

Before registering anything, the client MUST find out whether the network supports registration. It adds the option code to the Option Request option of its Information-Request, Solicit, Request, Renew or Rebind messages. A supporting server includes the option in its Advertise or Reply. If the infrastructure does not support registration, the client MUST NOT register addresses, to avoid undesired multicast traffic.

Once a client has a valid self-generated or statically configured address, it multicasts an ADDR-REG-INFORM message carrying one IA Address option for that address. The server logs it and replies with ADDR-REG-REPLY.
sections.plainLanguage: First the device asks, 'Do you take address reports here?' Only if the answer is yes does it send its report, and then it waits for a thank-you note.

sections.title: The Option and the Two Messages
sections.content:
The OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE option has code 148 and an option-len of 0. A client with registration enabled MUST include it in all Option Request options it sends, and a configured server MUST include it in Advertise and Reply messages when the client asked for it.

Two new DHCPv6 message types carry the registration. ADDR-REG-INFORM is message type 36 and ADDR-REG-REPLY is message type 37. Both use the usual DHCPv6 layout: a message type, a transaction ID and a variable list of options.

The inform message MUST include the Client Identifier option and exactly one IA Address option. It MUST NOT include a Server Identifier option or any Option Request option. The valid and preferred lifetimes in the IA Address option MUST match the address's current lifetimes. The client MAY add other options, such as Client FQDN.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two forms: a 'here is my address' form and a 'got it' form. The first has to name who is filling it in and which address, nothing more.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
The client sends ADDR-REG-INFORM to the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address ff02::1:2, with a separate message for each address. Unlike most DHCPv6 messages, it MUST be sent from the address being registered, not the link-local address. This is mainly for fate sharing: if the network stops MAC spoofing at layer 2, it also stops an attacker spoofing registrations. On a multi-interface client, the message goes only out the interface that holds the address.

Only valid addresses of global scope are registered, which includes Unique Local Addresses and statically assigned global addresses. Addresses configured by DHCPv6 MUST NOT be registered. The client SHOULD NOT send registrations unless it has seen a Router Advertisement with the M or O flag set to 1.

A server MUST discard a message that lacks a Client Identifier, has a Server Identifier, has no IA Address option or one that does not match the source address, or contains an Option Request. Otherwise the server SHOULD check that the address is appropriate to the link or within a prefix delegated to the client. If it passes, the server MUST log it (including the DUID and link-layer address where available), SHOULD create or update a binding lasting the reported Valid Lifetime, SHOULD mark the address unavailable for future Advertise messages, and MUST send an ADDR-REG-REPLY.
sections.plainLanguage: The device must send the note from the address it is reporting, like writing your own return address on the envelope. The office checks the note makes sense, writes it down and sends back a reply.

sections.title: The Reply and Retransmission
sections.content:
The server answers with ADDR-REG-REPLY, copying the transaction ID and including an IA Address option identical to the one it received. If the inform was not relayed, the reply goes to the registered address. The client MUST discard a reply whose destination, IA Address option, receiving interface or transaction ID does not match.

The reply only means the message arrived and need not be retransmitted. It MUST NOT be treated as a sign the address is valid and is not required for the address to be usable. Relays and snooping devices MUST NOT change forwarding or security state because of it.

Because packets can be lost, the client MUST retransmit, following Section 15 of RFC 8415 with an initial retransmission time of 1 second and a maximum retransmission count of 3. These SHOULD be configurable. The transaction ID stays the same across retransmissions, the lifetimes are updated, and retransmission stops when a reply arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply is just a 'message received' stamp. It does not make the address legal. If no stamp comes back, the device tries again a few times.

sections.title: Expiry and Refresh
sections.content:
The client MUST refresh registrations so the server knows which addresses are still valid. For a SLAAC address, the refresh interval is 80% of the current Valid Lifetime, multiplied by a random value between 0.9 and 1.1 chosen when registration starts, so many clients do not refresh at the same moment. If a Router Advertisement changes an address's Valid Lifetime by more than 1%, the client recalculates and schedules a refresh. If the network never changes the lifetime, no refreshes are needed.

A statically assigned address has an infinite lifetime, so it is refreshed every StaticAddrRegRefreshInterval, which defaults to 4 hours and SHOULD be configurable. When refreshing, the client MAY also refresh addresses due within the next AddrRegRefreshCoalesce seconds, with a suggested default of 60, and MUST use a new transaction ID.

When a binding expires, the server MUST remove it and treat the address as available. A client MAY announce that it stopped using an address by sending an inform with both lifetimes set to zero, and the server then MUST act as if the address expired.
sections.plainLanguage: Like renewing a library card before it runs out: the device re-reports its address a bit before the old report expires, at slightly random times so everyone does not queue at once.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Limits
sections.content:
An attacker might register many addresses quickly to overwhelm the server or fill its logs, much like existing attacks that spoof DUIDs. If the network uses First-Come, First-Served SAVI, the server can trust that the sender really holds the address.

The mechanism is informational and meant to aid troubleshooting and forensics. A malicious or compromised device can simply not send the message, so it is not a strong access control, and the message MUST NOT be used for authentication or authorization.

On the privacy side, without MLD snooping link-local multicast is effectively broadcast, so an on-link attacker could see registration messages. Since they contain unique identifiers such as the DUID, the attacker may link addresses to one client even if it uses randomized MAC addresses. The RFC notes this is not specific to this mechanism and points to RFC 7844 for mitigation.
sections.plainLanguage: The list helps the office look back at what happened, but a sneaky device can skip reporting, so the list cannot be used as a lock on the door.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA allocated one DHCPv6 option and two message types in the DHCPv6 registry group. The option is OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE with value 148, which is a client ORO option and a singleton option. The messages are ADDR-REG-INFORM with value 36 and ADDR-REG-REPLY with value 37.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of DHCPv6 words got three new entries so everyone uses the same numbers for them.

messages.label: INFORMATION-REQUEST or SOLICIT
messages.note: Option Request lists OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE; sent from the link-local address.

messages.label: ADDR-REG-INFORM
messages.note: Sent from the address being registered; the server registers and logs it.

items.label: OPTION_ADDR_REG_ENABLE
items.desc: Option showing a server supports address registration; option-len is 0.

items.label: ADDR-REG-INFORM
items.desc: Client tells the server about an address it is using.

items.label: ADDR-REG-REPLY
items.desc: Server acknowledges receipt so the client stops retransmitting.
